newsitem.title: ITALY: Profits up 12 pct at Italy's Stet before sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Profits up 12 pct at Italy's Stet before sell-off.

text.p: Italian state telecoms holding Stet, due to be privatisated in early 1997, said group pre-tax profits climbed 12 percent in the first half of 1996 and promised a substantial improvement in full year results.

Stet, which holds majority stakes in telephone operator Telecom Italia and cellular phone firm Telecom Italia Mobile, said its pre-tax profit in the first six months of the year hit 4.04 trillion lire ($2.67 billion).
Turnover at the company, which is itself controlled by giant state holding IRI, climbed nine percent over the same period to 19.64 trillion lire.

"Forecasts for the full year envisage sales of around 40 trillion lire against 37.37 trillion lire in 1995," Stet said in a statement. "This leads us to see an economic performance for this year which will be significantly better than in 1995."
Stet's pre-tax profit was 5.78 trillion lire last year.

The group, which is headed by Ernesto Pascale, said it was undertaking a mammoth investment programme to prepare the company for the full liberalisation of the telecommunications market in the year 2000.

It said investments in the first half rose to 4.6 trillion lire from 3.5 trillion lire in the same period last year. Between 1997 and 1999, it intended to plunge a further 35.5 trillion lire into investments, Stet said.
This programme will be self-financed allowing the group to cut its debt, Stet said. In the first half of 1996 debt fell to 14.3 trillion lire from 15.4 trillion at the end of 1995.
Much of the investment will go towards upgrading technology at Telecom Italia and TIM, but around four trillion lire has been earmarked to develop Stet's international ambitions.

Stet has focused much of its foreign expansion efforts in Latin America and Europe as well as in parts of Asia, but unlike many of its major European rivals, it has so far failed to find a large international telecoms partner.

Managing director Pascale said earlier this year that his company was in "very close talks" with both UK telecom firm Cable and Wireless and France's Bouygues group over the formation of alliances in the sector.
It is also involved in long-running talks with U.S. computer giant IBM over a planned global communications deal. Stet made no mention of any of these negotiations on Wednesday.
The government is anxious for the firm to secure a presitigious ally to boost the company's appeal ahead of the planned privatisation.
The Treasury announced in August it wanted debt-ladden IRI to float its remaining 64 percent stake in Stet by March 31, 1997, in a sale which has been dubbed "the mother of all privatisations".

Before the sell-off process can begin, parliament has to set up a watchdog body to cover the telecoms sector. The government hopes the necessary legislation will be ratified by Christmas, but the bill is tied to a controversial draft law on television ownership which may delay ratification.

In the meantime, the government has ordered Stet to sell its non-core publishing division Seat before the privatisation. Newspapers have reported that 20 international firms, including U.S. group GTE, are lining up to buy Stet's 61 percent stake. $1 = 1,513 lire
